title: Chief Economists' Outlook: September 2026
gist: The WEF's September 2026 Chief Economists' Outlook is more stable in tone than the May edition, but flags geopolitical conflict and asset-price corrections as top risks and warns that fiscal support, the key source of resilience since 2020, will matter less because governments have less room to respond. India and South-East Asia rank strongest, the US moderate, China weakening and Europe lowest. AI is still the main source of optimism, but data-centre expansion is expected to meet local pushback, push up utility costs and create few jobs.

themes.theme: Shrinking fiscal backstop and tail risks

insights.claim: Surveyed chief economists in the WEF's September 2026 Chief Economists' Outlook name geopolitical conflict and asset-price corrections among their most prominent concerns, even though the overall tone is more stable than the May 2026 edition.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The calmer headline sentiment sits alongside an explicit asset-correction risk, so don't read the better tone as the all-clear for adding risk. Keep hedges against drawdowns.

insights.claim: Fiscal support has been the key source of economic resilience since 2020, but chief economists expect it to play a smaller role in future shocks because governments have less room to respond.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: With less fiscal cushion, the next downturn or asset correction may go deeper and last longer than the 2020-era playbook implies. Price more downside tail and less policy rescue into risk assets and credit.
insights.quote: Fiscal support is considered the key source of resilience since 2020, but is expected to play a smaller role as governments have less room to respond.

insights.claim: Chief economists give India and South-East Asia the strongest regional growth assessments, expect moderate growth in the US, see China's outlook weakening, and still rank Europe as the region with the lowest growth expectations despite a modest improvement.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The consensus ranking supports overweighting India and ASEAN relative to China and Europe. Because it is consensus, the contrarian opportunity is in any Europe or China upside surprise.

insights.claim: Cost-of-living pressures persist, with real incomes stagnant or falling across most regions, according to the WEF's chief economists.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Flat or falling real incomes limit consumer volume growth and keep political pressure on prices high. That favours value and discount consumer exposure over discretionary.

insights.claim: Trade and investment flows keep adapting even as geoeconomic fragmentation deepens, so fragmentation is rerouting activity rather than stopping it.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Favour the beneficiaries of rerouted supply chains, the connector economies such as India and South-East Asia, over a blanket de-globalisation short.
insights.quote: Trade and investment continue to adapt even as geoeconomic fragmentation deepens.

insights.claim: Artificial intelligence remains chief economists' leading source of economic optimism, yet they call the outlook for AI-related investment uncertain.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Optimism about AI as a theme and uncertainty about the capex path can coexist. Watch for a gap opening between AI narrative and investment spending as a risk to AI-infrastructure equities.

insights.claim: Chief economists expect data-centre expansion to meet local pushback, raise utility costs and create only limited jobs. A related WEF piece describes AI data centres as driving a big part of growth in the year ahead but facing 'significant' local backlash.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Local permitting and political resistance are a timing risk for hyperscaler and data-centre build-outs. Rising utility bills may bring regulators in to push grid costs back onto data-centre operators.
insights.quote: data centre expansion is expected to face local pushback and bring higher utility costs and limited job creation
